questions.q: In hydrogen spectrum, if the shortest wavelength in Balmer series is $\lambda$, the shortest wavelength in Brackett series is
questions.solution:
For Balmer series,
$\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{Balmer }}}=R \left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right), where $n=3,4,5 \ldots$
For shortest wavelength, $n=$\infty\begin{array}{rlrl}\Rightarrow$& $\frac{1}{\lambda}$& =R$\left(\frac{1}{2^2}\right)=\frac{R}{4}$\\ $\text{ or }$& \lambda=$\frac{4}{R}\end{array}
For Brackett series,
\frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{Brackett }}}=$R $\left(\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)$, where $n=5,6,7, \ldots$
Again, for shortest wavelength, $n=\infty\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{Brackett }}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4^2}\right)=\frac{R}{16} \\ & \text{ or } \lambda_{\text{Brackett }}=\frac{16}{R}=4\left(\frac{4}{R}\right)=4 \lambda\end{aligned}$
[From Eq. (i)]

questions.solution:
Energy of ${H}_{\alpha}$-light

$= - 13. 6\left[\dfrac{1}{32} - \dfrac{1}{22}\right]eV = - 13. 6\left[\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right]eV \approx 1. 89eV$

Maximum work function of the metal should be equal to this value for it to emit photoelectrons from it.

questions.q: A hydrogen sample is prepared in a particular excited state $A$ of quantum number, $n_A=3$. The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is $-|E|$. The photons of energy $\frac{|E|}{12}$ are absorbed in the sample which results in the excitation of some electrons to excited state $B$ of quantum number $n_B$, whose value is
questions.solution: Given, energy of hydrogen atom in ground state =-|E| and $n_A=3 \therefore$ Energy of electrons in excited state, $n_A (E)_{n_A}=\frac{-|E|}{n_A^2}$Energy of electrons in excited state, $n_B =(E)_{n B}=\frac{-(E)}{n_B^2}$When sample absorbs the photon of energy, $\frac{|E|}{12}$, then its electrons reaches from energy state $n_A$ to energy state $n_B$.$\begin{aligned} \\ & \text{ Hence, }(E)_{n_B}-(E)_{n_A}=\frac{|E|}{12} \\ \\ & \frac{-|E|}{n_B^2}-\left\{\frac{-|E|}{n_A^2}\right\}=\frac{|E|}{12} \\ \\ & \frac{-1}{n_B^2}+\frac{1}{n_A^2}=\frac{1}{12} \Rightarrow-\frac{1}{n_B^2}=\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{n_A^2} \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{9} \Rightarrow-\frac{1}{n_B^2}=-\frac{1}{36} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow n_B^2=36 \\ \\ & \therefore n_B=6 \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The frequency of light emitted, when the electron makes transition from the level of principle quantum number $n=2$ to the level with $n=1$ is (Take, the ionization energy of hydrogen to be $13.6 \mathrm{eV}$ and $h \simeq 4 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{eV}$-s)
questions.solution:
As ionisation energy is $13.6 \mathrm{eV}$, so its negative will be the energy of atom in ground state $(n=1)$ hence $B_1=-136 \mathrm{eV}$
Energy in second orbit $(n=1)$
$B_2=-\frac{13.6}{2^2}=-3.4 \mathrm{eV}$
When electron jumps from $n=2 to n=1$, then energy of photon emitted by atom
$\begin{aligned} \\ \Delta E & =B_2-B_1 \\ \\ & =-3.4-(-13.6) \\ \\ \Delta B & =10.2 \mathrm{eV} \\ \end{aligned}$
So, frequency (v),
$\begin{aligned} \\ h v & =10.2 \mathrm{eV} \\ \\ v & =\frac{10.2 \mathrm{eV}}{h}=\frac{10.2 \mathrm{eV}}{4 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{s}} \\ \\ v & =255 \times 10^{+15} \mathrm{ Hz} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the series limit frequency of Balmer series is ${ν}_{B}$, then the series limit frequency of the Brackett series is
questions.solution:
As we know, wavelength of the light emitted during transition is given by,

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left[\dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{1}\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{2}\right)}^{2}}\right]$.

Frequency can be written as,

$ν = cR\left[\dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{1}\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{2}\right)}^{2}}\right]$

Now, for Balmer series$\left(2\text{to} \infty\right)$,

${ν}_{B} = cR\left[\dfrac{1}{{\left(2\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left(\infty\right)}^{2}}\right] . . . . Eq\left(1\right)$

For Brackett series we can write$\left(4\text{to} \infty\right)$,

${ν}^{'} = cR\left[\dfrac{1}{{\left(4\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left(\infty\right)}^{2}}\right] . . . . Eq\left(2\right)$

From equation 2 and equation 1, we get

$\dfrac{{ν}^{'}}{{ν}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{4} ⇒ {ν}^{'} = \dfrac{{ν}_{B}}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the Bohr model an electron of mass $m$ moves in a circular orbit around the proton. Considering the orbiting electron to be a circular current loop, the magnetic moment of the hydrogen atom, when the electron is in $n$ th excited state. (Assume, $h=$ Planck's constant)
questions.solution:
If $R$ be the radius of circular path, then magnetic moment,
$M=i \times A=(e \times f) \times\left(\pi R^2\right) \quad\left(\because i=\frac{e}{T}=e f\right)=e \times\left(\frac{v}{2 \pi R}\right) \times\left(\pi R^2\right)\left[\because \omega=2 \pi f \Rightarrow \frac{V}{R}=2 \pi f \Rightarrow f=\frac{V}{2 \pi R}\right]\Rightarrow \quad M=\frac{e v R}{2}\ldots$ (i)
Now, using Bohr's principle, Angular momentum, $L=m v R=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}\Rightarrow \quad v R=\frac{n h}{2 \pi m}\ldots$ (ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$M=\frac{e}{2} \times  \left(\frac{n h}{2 \pi m}\right)= \left(\frac{e}{2 m}\right) \times\left(\frac{n h}{2 \pi}\right)$

questions.q:
The phase difference between the following two waves ${y}_{2}$ and ${y}_{1}$ is:

${y}_{1} = asin \left(\omegat -kx\right)$

${y}_{2} = bcos \left(\omegat -$ kx + $\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given: ${y}_{1} = asin\left(\omegat - kx\right)$ and ${y}_{2} = bcos\left(\omegat - kx + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

${y}_{2} = bcos\left(\omegat - kx + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = bsin\left(\omegat - kx + \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

${y}_{2} = bsin\left(\omegat - kx + \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$

The phase difference between ${y}_{2} = bsin\left(\omegat - kx + \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ and ${y}_{1} = asin\left(\omegat - kx\right)$ is equal to $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

questions.q:
Blue light travelling in a vacuum has a wavelength of $450nm.$ It enters a medium whose refractive index is $1. 5.$ What is its frequency in the medium?
(Speed of light in vacuum $= 3 \times {10}^{8}ms^{- 1}$)
questions.solution:
The wavelength of blue light is,& $\lambda = 450 \times {10}^{- 9}m$ and the refractive index,& $n = 1 . 5$, the relation between refractive index and wavelength,
$\dfrac{\lambda1}{\lambda2} = \dfrac{n2}{n1}⇒ \dfrac{450}{\lambda2} = \dfrac{1 . 5}{1} ⇒ {λ}_{2} = 300nm$,

then the frequency of refracted light is,
${f}_{2} = \dfrac{v}{\lambda2} = \dfrac{c}{n{λ}_{2}} = \dfrac{3 \times {10}^{8}}{1 . 5 \times 300 \times {10}^{- 9}} = 6 . 67 \times {10}^{14}Hz$

A light bulb of power $100W$ is placed at the centre of a hollow sphere of radius $10cm.$ If the $66 %$ of the energy is converted into light, then the pressure exerted by the light on the surface of the sphere will be
(Assume the surface of sphere to be perfectly absorbing)
questions.solution:
Intensity of bulb at $r = 10cm$, we have
$I = \dfrac{P}{4\pir^{2}}$
Intensity of bulb, that is converted to light is, $I ' = 0. 66I$
$⇒ I ' = 0. 66 \times \dfrac{P}{4\pir^{2}}$

Radiation pressure in this case is given by, $Pr = \dfrac{I '}{c}$, as light is absorbed at the surface of sphere.
$⇒ Pr = \dfrac{0. 66}{c} \times \dfrac{P}{4\pir^{2}}$
$⇒ Pr = \dfrac{0. 66}{3 \times {10}^{8}} \times \dfrac{100}{4\pi \times 0. {10}^{2}} = 1. 75 \times {10}^{- 6}Nm^{- 2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The collision of an electron with kinetic energy $5.5 \mathrm{eV}$ and a hydrogen atom in its ground state can be described as
questions.solution:
Given, kinetic energy of electron $=5.5 \mathrm{eV}$.
The energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from ground state $(n=1)$ to first excited state $(n=2)$ is
$\begin{aligned}
\Delta E & =E_2-E_2 \\
& =-3.4-(-13.6)=10.2 \mathrm{eV}
\end{aligned}$
When an electron collides with hydrogen atom in the ground state with energy of $5.5 \mathrm{eV}$ which is less than $10.2 \mathrm{eV}$, then it will not be able to excite hydrogen atom in to first excited state. Therefore, electron will not give any energy to the hydrogen atom. Hence, the total kinetic energy of electron remains conserved. Hence, its collision with hydrogen atom is elastic.

questions.q: Monochromatic radiation is incident on hydrogen $(\mathrm{H})$ sample which is in ground state. If the hydrogen atoms emit radiation of ten different wavelengths after absorbing the incident radiation, then the wavelength of the incident radiation is (Let $h c=1242$ eV-nm)
questions.solution:
Given, $h c=1242 \mathrm{eV} \cdot \mathrm{nm}$
Since, monochromatic radiation is incident on hydrogen sample which is in ground state.
Hence, the energy of ground state is given by
$\begin{aligned} & |E|=13.6 \mathrm{eV} \\ & \frac{h c}{\lambda}=13.6 \\ & \lambda=\frac{h c}{136}=\frac{1242}{13.6} \mathrm{ nm} \\ & =91.3 \mathrm{ nm}-95.1 \mathrm{ nm}\end{aligned}$
Hence, the wavelength of incident radiation is $95.1 \mathrm{ nm}$.

questions.q: The ratio of longest wavelengths of the spectral lines in the Lyman and Balmer series of hydrogen spectrum is
questions.solution:
The longest wavelength for Lyman series $(2 \rightarrow 1)\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{L}}}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{(1)^2}-\frac{1}{(2)^2}\right)=\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{R}$
And for Balmer series $(3 \rightarrow 2)\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{(2)^2}-\frac{1}{(3)^2}\right)=\frac{5}{36} \mathrm{R} \\ & \therefore \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{L}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A monochromatic radiation of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a hydrogen sample in ground state. The sample subsequently emits radiation of six different wavelengths, then the value of $\lambda$ is
[Use ch $=1242 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{m}$ ]
questions.solution:
Number of line emitted $=6, n_i=1, n_f=4$
$\begin{aligned} \\ \frac{n(n-1)}{2} & =6 \\ \\ n^2-n-12 & =0 \\ \\ (n-4)(n+3) & =0 \\ \\ n=4, n & =-3 \quad \text{(Not possible)} \\ \end{aligned}$
Using, $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{n_i^2}-\frac{1}{n_f^2}\right)}$
$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right)=R \frac{15}{16}$
where, $R=1.09 \times 10^7 \mathrm{ m}^{-1}$
$\lambda=\frac{16}{15} \times \frac{1}{1.09 \times 10^7}=97.4 \mathrm{ nm}$

questions.q: Let $\lambda_P$ and $\lambda_L$ be the longest wavelengths observed in the Paschen and Lyman series respectively. Choose the correct option
questions.solution:
As we know, wavelength for Paschen-series.
$\frac{1}{\lambda_P}=R\left[\frac{1}{3^2}-\frac{1}{n_p^2}\right], n_p=4,5,6$
and wavelength for Lyman-series,
$\frac{1}{\lambda_L}=R\left[1-\frac{1}{n_L^2}\right], n_L=2,3,4 \ldots$
Hence, $\lambda_p$ for $n_p=4$
$\frac{1}{\lambda_p}=R\left[\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16}\right],=\frac{7 R}{9 \times 16}$
and $\lambda_L$ for $n_L=2$
$\frac{1}{\lambda_L}=R\left[1-\frac{1}{4}\right]=\frac{3 R}{4}$
From Eq. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_L}=\frac{3 R / 4}{7 R / 9 \times 16}=15.42$
So, $15 < \frac{\lambda_P}{\lambda_L} < 16$
Hence, the correct option is (c).

questions.q: For an $EM$ Wave, the electric and magnetic fields are $300Vm^{- 1}$ and $7. 9Am^{- 1}$ respectively. The maximum rate of energy flow is,&
questions.solution: Here, the amplitude of the electric field, ${E}_{0} = 300Vm^{- 1}$; the amplitude of the magnetic field, ${H}_{0} = 7. 9Am^{- 1}$. We know that the maximum rate of energy flows in terms of the amplitude of the electric field and magnetic field, $S = {E}_{0} \times {H}_{0} = 300 \times 7. 9 = 2370Wm^{- 2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of a spectral line emitted by hydrogen atom in the Balmer series is $\frac{16}{3 R}$ ( $R$ is Rydberg constant). What is the value of the principal quantum number of the state from which the transition takes place?
questions.solution:
In spectral line series, wavelength is given by $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R \left(\frac{1}{n_f^2}-\frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)$ For $Balmer transitions,
$\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{1}{\lambda}= R \left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right) Given, $\quad \$lambda=\frac{16}{3 R}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{3 R}{16}=$R$\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{3}{16}=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{n^2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{n^2}=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{16}=\frac{1}{16} \Rightarrow$n=4$

questions.q: An electron collides with a hydrogen atom in its grownd state and excites it to $n=3$ state. The energy given to the hydrogen atom in this inelastic collision (neglecting the recoil of hydrogen atom) is
questions.solution:
According to the question,
Energy given to hydrogen atom $=$ Difference in energy level from $n_1=1$ to $n_2=3$ states
$=13.6\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)=13.6 \left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{3^2}\right)=13.6\left(1-\frac{1}{9}\right)<$ br />$=13.6 \times \frac{8}{9}=12.08 $\approx$12.1 \mathrm{eV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The radius of the first orbit of hydrogen is $\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{H}}$, and the energy in the ground state is - $13.6 \mathrm{eV}$. Considering a $\mu^{-}$-particle with a mass $207 m_e$ revolving round a proton as in hydrogen atom, the energy and radius of proton and $\mu^{-}$- combination respectively in the first orbit are (assume nucleus to be stationary)
questions.solution:
The total energy of $n$th orbit
$E_n=-\frac{m e^4}{8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^2} \cdot \frac{1}{n^2}$
Obviously $E_n \propto m$
$\begin{array}{llll} \\ & \therefore & \frac{E_\mu}{E_e} & =\frac{m_\mu}{m_e} \\ \\ \Rightarrow & E_\mu & =\frac{m_\mu}{m_e} \times E_e \\ \end{array} \\ Ground state energy of a proton in hydrogen atom, \\ \begin{aligned}$
E_\mu & =-13.6 $\times \frac{207 m_e}{m_e} \mathrm{eV}$\\
& =-13.6 $\times207 \mathrm{eV}$
\end{aligned}$ \\ \left(\because$ m_\mu=207 m_e\right.$, where $m_e$ is the mass of electron $)$ \\ We know that \\ $r=$\frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2 n^2}{207 \pi m_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{e}^2} \\ For ground state $(n-1)$ for proton, we have \\ $r_\mu=$\frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2}{207 \pi m_e \cdot e^2} \\ But \frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2}{\pi m_{\mathrm{e}} \cdot e^2}= ground state radius of hydrogen atom \\ \begin{aligned}$
$\frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2}{\pi m_e \cdot e^2}$& $=r_{\mathrm{H}$} \\
\therefore \quad r_\mu & =$\frac{r_{\mathrm{H}}}{207}$
\end{aligned}
